title: What was the Silk Road actually for?
subtitle: Horses, silk and microbes
subject: histoire
description: A Chinese emperor wanted horses and allies. Without knowing it, he opened the corridor through which silk, Buddhism, smallpox and plague crossed Eurasia.
author: ezgi-gizem-berkay

hero.hook: Neither the merchant nor the plague traveled the whole road: they moved in relays, from one stop to the next.

blocks.text: No emperor decreed its path, and no engineer drew its course on a map. The Silk Road was never a single road: it was a web of tracks that time turned into a legend. Why was it opened, and what did it become? Two different questions: one is about an intention, the other about an outcome that went far beyond it.

Contrary to popular belief, the route was born of military and diplomatic needs. In the **2nd century BC**, Emperor Wu of China's Han dynasty sent his envoy [[Zhang Qian]] westward to find allies against the [[Xiongnu]], nomads who threatened the north of the empire. On his return, Zhang Qian described the cities and riches of Central Asia, and above all the legendary "Celestial Horses" of [[Fergana]].

sections.title: From silk to microbes: a fatal relay

blocks.text: These horses mattered so much to the Han army that Wu launched two major campaigns against Fergana between **104 and 101 BC**: the "War of the Celestial Horses." Once open, the route quickly outgrew its purpose. Beyond silk, people traded horses, glassware, precious stones, spices, paper and metalwork. In Rome, silk became the most coveted luxury and the symbol of the whole network.

blocks.caption: A Buddhist mural from the Mogao Caves at Dunhuang (Tang period).

blocks.text: The name is recent: in **1877**, the German geographer Ferdinand von Richthofen christened these tracks the "Seidenstraße," the Silk Road. Before him, East and West had crossed these sands without giving a name to the ties they wove.

Along with the goods traveled people and ideas: Buddhism entered China, and techniques and artistic styles spread. But the deadliest cargo was invisible. Pathogens passed from hand to hand as fast as silks and spices. Neither the merchant nor the plague traveled the whole length of the road: they moved in relays, each stop passing the contagion to the next. Travelers and their pack animals were the main carriers.

Two great epidemics that shook the Roman Empire are closely tied to the eastern trade routes. The first was the [[Antonine Plague]], from **165 to 180**. Historians generally identify it as smallpox, brought back by legions returning from campaigns against the Parthians. The epidemic scarred the reign of the emperor **Marcus Aurelius**, decimated the population and weakened the imperial army.

blocks.caption: Plague in Rome, by Jules-Élie Delaunay (1869, Musée d'Orsay): the exterminating angel strikes at a door.

blocks.text: Nearly a century later, the Plague of Cyprian struck in turn, from **249 to 262**. It is believed to have come from the East, but its exact nature is still debated: smallpox, measles or a viral hemorrhagic fever? One thing is certain: Rome's insatiable appetite for silk carried previously unknown pathogens westward.

sections.title: From Justinian to the Black Death

blocks.text: The Plague of Justinian, from **541 to 750**, is recognized as the first great pandemic of bubonic plague, caused by the bacterium [[Yersinia pestis]]. Accounts of the time place its starting point at Pelusium, in Egypt. But its true origins lie elsewhere: ancient DNA sequencing has established that the bacterium came from Central Asia and spread westward along the trade routes.

blocks.caption: The bacterium Yersinia pestis, the cause of plague, under the electron microscope.

blocks.text: The most famous example of this mechanism is the Black Death of the **14th century**, the second pandemic of Yersinia pestis. It broke out just as the Mongol Empire secured and unified these trade networks: the [[Pax Mongolica]]. The same infrastructure sped up the disease, from Central Asia toward the West. Between **1347 and 1351**, the pandemic wiped out one-third to one-half of Europe's population.

sections.title: The microbial unification of the world

blocks.text: The road did not spread only great epidemics. It also carried endemic, silent diseases that took root wherever they arrived: leprosy, tuberculosis, intestinal parasites. The pattern is always the same: worlds long kept apart pooled their microbes along with their goods.

Historians call this phenomenon the [[microbial unification of the world]], or the convergence of disease pools. The phrase was coined by the French historian **Emmanuel Le Roy Ladurie** in **1973**. Three years later, in *Plagues and Peoples* (1976), the historian **William McNeill** laid the groundwork for a history of the ties between diseases and human societies.

So what was the Silk Road really for? To bring horses and allies to a Chinese emperor. What it became: a corridor traveled by silk, Buddhism and paper, but also by smallpox and plague. Its most lasting effects were neither wanted nor foreseen.
Opened by the Han for horses and alliances, the Silk Road became the corridor that pooled the goods, ideas and microbes of Eurasia, from the Antonine Plague to the Black Death.
